results.summary: Security review of sample-java-code found no injection, hardcoded secrets, unsafe deserialization, Struts remnants, or entity mass-assignment patterns. The app still fails the security gate because the public API lacks explicit request-size DoS protection, security headers, and rate limiting in the reviewed target.

findings.category: Denial of Service / OWASP A05 Security Misconfiguration
findings.title: No explicit request body size limit for public JSON endpoint
findings.description: The public POST /api/greetings endpoint accepts a JSON request body, but the reviewed Spring Boot configuration does not define request body, swallow, multipart, or proxy-level limits. Bean Validation @Size(max = 40) runs only after the request body has already been read and parsed, so oversized requests can still consume memory or connection resources before validation rejects the logical field value.
findings.evidence: application.yml only configures server.port and spring.application.name. GreetingController exposes @PostMapping("/greetings") with @RequestBody at sample-java-code/src/main/java/com/codexskishop/sample/api/GreetingController.java:57-58. Targeted rg searches found no max request body, multipart, Tomcat swallow, timeout, gateway, or rate-limit configuration.
findings.suggestedFix: Add explicit request limits in application.yml and enforce JSON body limits at the servlet filter, embedded server, gateway, or reverse proxy layer. Example: set server.tomcat.max-swallow-size, server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size, spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size/request-size, connection timeouts, and add a small max-body filter for application/json requests.

findings.category: Security Headers / OWASP A05 Security Misconfiguration
findings.title: Security headers are not configured
findings.description: The application has no Spring Security dependency or SecurityFilterChain, and application.yml does not configure equivalent HTTP header hardening. Responses therefore lack an in-target defense for CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, HSTS, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, and server header suppression. Even for a small public API, these headers are part of the repository's security review standard and reduce browser-based attack impact when endpoints are consumed directly.
findings.evidence: pom.xml includes validation, web, and test starters only; no spring-boot-starter-security. application.yml lines 1-6 contain no server-header or header policy configuration. Targeted rg search found no SecurityFilterChain, contentSecurityPolicy, frameOptions, HSTS, referrerPolicy, or permissionsPolicy configuration.
findings.suggestedFix: Add spring-boot-starter-security and define a SecurityFilterChain that explicitly permits intended public endpoints while configuring headers: contentTypeOptions, frameOptions deny, CSP default-src 'self', HSTS for TLS deployments, strict-origin-when-cross-origin referrer policy, and permissionsPolicy camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(). Also set server.server-header to blank where supported.

findings.title: Public endpoints have no rate limiting
findings.description: GET /api/greetings and POST /api/greetings are unauthenticated public endpoints and no rate limiting, throttling filter, or gateway policy is present in the reviewed target. The endpoint is simple, but attackers can still flood it to consume request threads and CPU, especially because POST requires JSON parsing and validation.
findings.evidence: GreetingController exposes public GET and POST greeting endpoints. Targeted rg search found no Bucket4j, RateLimiter, rate-limit filter, Spring Cloud Gateway policy, or equivalent throttling configuration in sample-java-code/src/main or pom.xml.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a small rate-limiting filter or gateway policy for /api/**, with stricter limits for state-changing methods. For this sample, a per-IP token bucket with conservative defaults and 429 responses is sufficient.

findings.title: Production error disclosure settings are not explicit
findings.description: The global exception handler sanitizes validation errors, which is good, but the runtime configuration does not explicitly lock down Spring Boot error disclosure settings. Defaults may be safe today, but OSS-quality production configuration should pin server.error.include-stacktrace and server.error.include-message to never so future profile or dependency changes do not expose internal exception details.
findings.evidence: application.yml contains only port and application name. GlobalExceptionHandler handles validation exceptions at sample-java-code/src/main/java/com/codexskishop/sample/api/GlobalExceptionHandler.java:24-49, but targeted rg found no include-stacktrace or include-message configuration.
findings.suggestedFix: Add server.error.include-stacktrace: never, server.error.include-message: never, and server.error.include-binding-errors: never for production-like profiles. Keep validation responses generic as currently implemented.

escalations.description: Decide whether sample-java-code is intentionally a fully public demo API. If yes, document that choice and explicitly permit only /api/health and /api/greetings in SecurityFilterChain while still applying headers, request limits, and rate limiting. If no, add default-deny authentication before publishing.

| # | Attack Scenario | Defense Exists | Risk | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SM-1..SM-5 | Session fixation, timeout, concurrent session, cookie flags | No session auth in target; no explicit cookie hardening | Medium if auth is added later | ⚠️ |
